// CellRelation describes the possible relationships between a target cell
// and the cells of the ShapeIndex. If the target is an index cell or is
// contained by an index cell, it is Indexed. If the target is subdivided
// into one or more index cells, it is Subdivided. Otherwise it is Disjoint.

	// cellPadding defines the total error when clipping an edge which comes

content.text:
`ShapeIndex` now has `Encode(io.Writer)` and `Decode(io.Reader)`. A decoded index can be queried and iterated immediately, with no `Build`. It's committed on a new branch, `shapeindex-encode` (commit `bed5618`). The repo has no `main` branch, only `master`, so I branched from `master`. The full test suite, `go vet` and `gofmt` all pass.

**What it does** (`s2/shapeindex_encode.go`):
- **Shapes:** each shape is stored under its original ID, so gaps left by removed shapes stay in place and cell references remain valid.
- **Built-in types:** all seven (`Polygon`, `Loop`, `Polyline`, `PointVector`, `LaxPolyline`, `LaxLoop`, `LaxPolygon`) decode back to the same Go type with the same edge order. This includes shapes with no edges, empty and full loops, and lax polygons with empty loops mixed in.
- **Other shapes:** anything else, such as test-only shapes, decodes as a generic internal shape with the same edges, chains, dimension and reference point, but not its original type.
- **Cell structure:** every cell is stored in full, with its list of shapes, edge IDs and whether its centre is inside each shape.
- **No `Build` needed before encoding:** `Encode` applies any pending updates first, and an empty index still produces a non-empty byte stream.
- **Bad input returns an error instead of panicking:** all lengths are capped and slices grow only as data actually arrives, so a fake huge length can't force a big allocation. Cells must be valid and in order, and must point at shapes and edges that exist. A failed `Decode` leaves the index unchanged, and a `recover` catches anything the checks miss.

**Testing** (`s2/shapeindex_encode_test.go`): the tests round-trip every shape type and check that edges, chains, cells, iteration and point-containment queries match the original. They also cover an empty index, zero-edge shapes, encoding without `Build`, and IDs surviving removals. Every possible truncation of an encoding fails, and hand-built inputs with huge lengths are rejected. I also ran a one-off fuzz pass of 100k mutated inputs (not committed): none panicked, and the 13.6k that decoded answered queries without crashing.

**Bug fix in `shapeindex.go`:** after any shape was removed, shapes added later were never indexed. The update loop counted up to the number of shapes instead of the next ID. I fixed it because decoded indexes with removed shapes would hit this.

**Problems in existing code I didn't fix** (they also occur on `master`):
- **Removed shapes stay in the cells:** `removeShapeInternal` is an empty TODO, so removed shapes are never cleared out. `Encode` skips those leftover entries, so a decoded index never points at a missing shape. This means its cells can be cleaner than the original's.
- **Adding shapes after a `Build` breaks:** this applies to any index, decoded or not. It can deadlock, because the update re-locks a mutex it already holds via `s.Iterator()` in `shrinkToFit`. Once that's fixed, it reaches `tracker.lowerBound`, which is just `panic("not implemented")`. Making this work means implementing incremental updates properly, so it's a separate piece of work.

The encoding is a format specific to this Go package and can't be read by the C++ S2 library. It starts with a version byte so the format can change later.
